items.body: شهدت نهاية مباراة مانشستر سيتي وضيفه نابولي، بملعب الاتحاد، أحداثا ساخنة واعتراضات كبيرة من لاعبي الفريق الإنجليزي وجماهيره. نجا مانشستر سيتي، من هزيمة كانت قريبه على أرضه وبين جماهيره، على يد نابولي، حيث خطف تعادلا قاتلا بنتيجة 2/2، في المباراة التي جمعتهما اليوم الثلاثاء، ضمن الجولة الخامسة لمرحلة الدوري ببطولة دوري أبطال أوروبا.  وبينما كانت المباراة في طريقها للانتهاء بفوز نابولي 2/1، سجل ريان شرقي هدف التعادل لمانشستر سيتي، في الدقيقة 86. وبعدها ضغط السيتي بكل قوة لتسجيل هدف الفوز لكن المباراة انتهت بالتعادل 2/2. وقالت صحيفة " ذا صن "، إن مباراة مانشستر سيتي ونابولي في دوري أبطال أوروبا، انتهت وسط جدل كبير، بعد أن أطلق الحكم صافرته قبل 25 ثانية من نهاية الوقت المحتسب بدلا من الضائع. وخطف رجال إنزو ماريسكا التعادل 2-2 من الإيطاليين في ملعب الاتحاد ليلة الثلاثاء، لكن لاعبي وجماهير السيتي كانوا غاضبين بعد إطلاق صافرة النهاية بينما لا يزال الوقت متبقياً على الساعة الداخلية، حيث بدأوا في الإشارة إلى الساعة. وقاد حارس المرمى جيانلويجي دوناروما موجة غضب لاعبي وجماهير السيتي وحصل على بطاقة صفراء بسبب احتجاجه من قبل الحكم إستفان كوفاتش. 😡 ENOUGH IS ENOUGH! items.title: Why Nobel physics prize winner Francis Halzen staked his career on an 'almost non-existent piece of reality'
items.summary: Live Science spoke with Nobel laureate Francis Halzen on how he got into physics "by accident" and built a neutrino detector that changed it forever.
items.body: When Francis Halzen first proposed burying a $271 million telescope deep beneath the South Pole, he expected to be laughed off stage. Four decades later, it won him a Nobel Prize. Consisting of thousands of light sensors strung like rosary beads inside a cubic kilometer (0.2 cubic miles) of pristine ice, his detector, aptly named IceCube, is not an obvious way to study the universe. But Halzen , a theoretical physicist at the University of Madison-Wisconsin, isn't looking for something obvious. His quarries are neutrinos , near-massless, chargeless, shapeshifters that are the most abundant material particles in existence. They form from nuclear processes and high-energy collisions, swarming out of our sun and whizzing from the outskirts of black holes. Yet though neutrinos stream through stars, planets, and us every second in their trillions, you still have a 75% chance of living your entire life without a single one striking an atom in your body . items.title: It's time to look at Uranus: How to see the solar system's strangest planet at its best this week
items.summary: On Wednesday (Nov. 25), the distant ice giant Uranus will be at its best and brightest. Here's when, where and how to look for the seventh planet.
items.body: One of the hardest planets to see in the solar system — the distant ice giant Uranus — reaches its annual opposition on Wednesday (Nov. 25), just a day after the Beaver Supermoon . It's the best time to see the seventh planet from the sun, but you'll need to use stargazing binoculars or a good backyard telescope to find it. Uranus is faint, slow-moving and rarely a target for casual stargazers. However, on Nov. 25, and, for a few weeks on either side, it will be at its closest point to Earth this year and will appear at its brightest, making it possible to spot. Opposition occurs when Earth passes between Uranus and the sun; Uranus will be "opposite" the sun, hence, "opposition." The moment of opposition will happen at 6 p.m. ET on Nov. 25, according to EarthSky . Consequently, Uranus will rise in the east around sunset, reach its highest point in the sky around midnight and set in the west around sunrise. You can find it in the constellation Taurus, close to the Pleiades open star cluster, also known as the Seven Sisters and M45. 'A new record in quantum error correction': Scientists say breakthrough brings powerful, fault-tolerant quantum computers closer to reality
items.summary: Quantinuum's Helios processor achieved a record-low failure rate of just 0.0005%, suggesting fault-tolerant quantum systems may need far fewer qubits than previously thought.
items.body: Scientists at Quantinuum say they've set a new record in quantum error correction that brings large-scale, fault-tolerant systems one step closer. The team claims their 98-qubit quantum system, Helios , demonstrated a failure rate of just 0.0005% in tests of its quantum memory, which is equivalent to an estimated five uncorrectable errors per million rounds of error checking. This rate bests the previous benchmark set by Google's 105-qubit Willow quantum chip , which demonstrated an estimated 772 uncorrectable errors per million rounds in comparable tests , for an error rate of 0.0772%. The result brings quantum computing closer to the "megaquop regime," where systems can run over a million operations without encountering an error, the researchers said. They detailed their findings in a study uploaded Oct. 16 to the arXiv preprint server. In a statement , Robin Blume-Kohout , co-director of Sandia National Laboratories' Quantum Performance Lab, called the achievement "a significant milestone that quantum computing researchers have been working toward for many years." items.summary: Archaeologists have found the remains of a 2,900-year-old sanctuary on an island mountaintop, where ancient Greeks may have worshipped the goddess Artemis.
items.body: The discovery of a 2,900-year-old mountaintop sanctuary on a Mediterranean island shows the ancient Greek veneration for high mountains and their link to the Greek gods, archaeologists say. The sanctuary was found during new excavations on Euboea, a very large island only about 30 miles (50 kilometers) northeast of Athens. The sanctuary did not include any buildings, such as a temple. Archaeologists think it was used for offerings and feasting by worshippers for hundreds of years, from about the ninth century B.C. until the first or second century A.D., during Imperial Roman times. "We know that in the ancient Greek world, religious life was not limited to large temples and urban sanctuaries," excavation leader Chloé Chezeaux , an archaeologist at the Swiss School of Archeology in Greece, told Live Science in an email. "There were also many places of worship in the countryside and in the mountains." "An exceptional concentration of pottery" Chezeaux led the excavations this year near the summit of Elatias, one of the highest peaks of Mount Olympus on Euboea. "The remaining manoeuvres have already been replanned, with no extra burns needed," Aschbacher said. The two probes are still on track to seprate on Dec. 9. (This article was updated at 11:40 a.m. ET on Nov. 24). After eight years slingshotting around the inner solar system, the joint European-Japanese spacecraft BepiColombo has finally entered into orbit around Mercury — becoming only the second mission ever to orbit the closest planet to the sun. Mission scientists confirmed on Saturday (Nov. 21) that the spacecraft reached Mercury's orbit and is transmitting data back to the ground team. However, the orbital insertion didn't go entirely as planned, European Space Agency (ESA) representatives said in a statement on Monday. Due to a software glitch, the spacecraft didn't fire its thrusters for the full 37 minutes required to slow its approach to Mercury. items.body: Tech companies are investing a lot of hope and money in rocks. Google, Microsoft, and others have committed hundreds of millions of dollars to get startups to spread crushed basalt, olivine, or other alkaline materials across farms, in an effort to capture carbon from the air and lock it away. A number of influential models have found that this approach, known as enhanced rock weathering (ERW), could eventually remove 3 billion to 8 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide per year, helping to slow or one day even reverse global warming. An additional promise is that these applications of rock could help farmers by improving the quality of their soil. But a pair of preprint studies set for release today raise serious questions about how much material could be added to that soil before it may actually reduce the crop yields that are essential to farmers’ livelihoods, MIT Technology Review can exclusively report.  Cutting back on the rock applications to prevent these negative effects would shrink the method’s carbon dioxide removal capacity, likely capping it at less than a billion tons per year. (Image credit: Alamy) QUICK FACTS Name: Hoxne 'Empress' pepper pot What it is: A silver spice dispenser Where it is from: Hoxne, Suffolk, England When it was made: A.D. 350 to 400 In 1992, a farmer in the village of Hoxne in southeastern England was searching for a lost hammer with a metal detector when he stumbled upon a massive hoard of more than 15,000 ancient Roman coins, jewelry and tableware. Among the artifacts in the Hoxne hoard was a silver spice container in the shape of an imperial lady. The artifact, named the Empress, is one of four pepper pots ("piperatoria" in Latin) discovered in the Hoxne hoard, according to the British Museum . The silver container stands about 4 inches (10 centimeters) tall and is decorated with gold around the woman's eyes, mouth, hair and accessories, including a scroll in her left hand. The woman's elaborate hairstyle helps date the creation of the pepper pot to the fourth century, but experts think the hoard may have been buried in the early fifth century, when Roman rule in Britain was ending. items.title: Impossible volcanic eruption spotted in deepest part of the ocean, perplexing scientists
items.summary: Scientists are perplexed at discovering the world's deepest explosive volcanic eruption at Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench.
items.body: A submersible mission to the deepest ocean trench on Earth has made a shocking discovery: the deepest pyroclastic volcanic flow ever found on the planet, in a place geologists didn't expect to see any volcanic activity. This evidence of a violent undersea eruption was found 20,000 feet (6,000 meters) below the ocean surface on the walls of the Challenger Deep, the deepest point of the Mariana Trench and the deepest part of the ocean. It was a "complete surprise," said Robert Stern , a professor emeritus of geosciences at the University of Texas at Dallas and first author of a new study describing the discovery. Typically, volcanic activity doesn't occur that close to an ocean trench, Stern told Live Science. And given the site's extreme depth, the lava that made the flow must have had some very strange chemistry. Normally, the intense pressure of seawater at these depths would prevent an explosive eruption, instead favoring a goopier, seeping type of flow. But the flows seen on the edge of the Challenger Deep were similar to the explosive, roiling gases that coated Pompeii in ash in A.D. 79. items.body: Archaeologists in Hungary have discovered a stash of more than 200 Celtic silver coins that are over 2,000 years old. It's one of the largest hoards found there in decades. Researchers unearthed the coins during excavations ahead of construction for an electrical substation in western Hungary between 2023 and 2025, according to a translated statement from the power company E.ON. The hoard dates to sometime between the late second century B.C. and the early first century B.C. The coin cache weighs roughly 4.4 pounds (2 kilograms). In today's market, it's worth more than $2,000 as raw silver alone, but its rarity and historical value effectively make it priceless, the statement said. The site was once part of a farm, and plowing there had unearthed several individual coins in recent decades, the statement said. During the latest excavations, archaeologists initially found a few coins and then searched the area with metal detectors, which led them to the coin hoard. The treasure had been packed inside a small ceramic vessel and sat about 16 inches (40 centimeters) below ground. In a paper published Oct. 22 in the journal Physical Review D , researchers used several mathematical modeling methods to propose a "pair-of-pants" topology for black holes . The hypothesis suggests that under extremely specific conditions, these dark behemoths could fragment into numerous less-massive black holes. "Understanding precisely what is forbidden, what is merely unlikely, and what becomes possible once the assumptions are relaxed is the central goal of this work," the researchers wrote in the paper. For example, it could help to explain black holes with masses that are too small to be formed through conventional astrophysical processes. items.summary: Astronomers once assumed galaxies were born before black holes, but giant black holes spotted in the early universe are forcing them to rethink their order of events.
items.body: Nearly every large galaxy is thought to have a supermassive black hole at its center. The Milky Way's black hole, known as Sagittarius A*, is enormous, weighing over 4 million times as much as the sun . But which came first: the black holes or the galaxies around them? Astronomers told Live Science that they thought they knew, but new observations mean they're no longer sure. Challenging the standard model For decades, the prevailing idea was that galaxies came first: Dying massive stars leave behind black holes that can merge and feed until they swell to millions of times the sun's mass, said Joseph Silk , an astrophysicist and professor at Johns Hopkins University. Then, in recent years, the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) began peering back at the early universe. "Recent observations are challenging this picture, or at least showing us that it cannot be the whole story," Roberto Maiolino , a professor of astrophysics at the University of Cambridge, told Live Science in an email. The new mouse studies revealed previously unknown aspects of the disease's biology that could point to new avenues for treatment. The condition has long been thought of as a disease of neurons, as it triggers neuron death in a part of the brain that's key to controlling movement. But the new findings highlight an unsung role of neurons' support cells, called glial cells. "This had never been described in this disease before," study co-author Shane Liddelow , an associate professor in the Institute for Translational Neuroscience at the NYU Grossman School of Medicine, said of the new findings. "It really sort of upended this idea of the disease" as primarily affecting neurons. items.title: Why do wolves howl?
items.summary: Wolves howl for a variety of reasons. But none of them are triggered by the sight of the moon.
items.body: Wolves can bark, whimper, yip, squeak and growl , but they are most known for their iconic howl. The eerie sound can travel vast distances and, if heard by other wolves, get them to join in with the chorus. But why do wolves howl in the first place? Experts told Live Science that the behavior is triggered not by the sight of the moon, as is commonly believed, but by the need to maintain a complex social network. Howl you doin'? Wolves can howl by themselves and in groups. "If a lone wolf howls, it's probably because they're separated from their pack and want to regain contact," Arik Kershenbaum , a zoologist at the University of Cambridge, told Live Science. "Members of a pack can become quite dispersed, and when they need to hunt together, or to care for pups, or when their territory is being threatened by other wolves, they need a way of returning to each other." However, lone wolves that leave their packs may howl as well. This could be "a way of finding a new pack or mate to join," Kershenbaum said. items.body: A study of hundreds of brains has revealed molecular differences in people with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) that are not found in individuals without the condition. These molecular marks also differ from those seen in the brains of people with other conditions, like depression, the research found. Our environment and experiences influence how our genes work, affecting which genes can be turned on. Rather than changing genes' underlying code, the environment can trigger what are known as epigenetic changes , which include certain chemicals that attach to DNA molecules and change their structure. One such epigenetic change, called methylation, can work like a "dimmer switch" for genes, or even completely block certain genes from turning on. "These epigenetic features of the brain are important for shaping the way the brain functions," study co-author Frances Champagne , a psychologist at the University of Texas at Austin, told Live Science. "This can give us some insight into why individuals with PTSD develop PTSD, or how [their brains] are different from a healthy brain." items.body: A new study has rewritten the role of one of the brain's major speech hubs, opening new possibilities for treating people who can't communicate verbally due to brain damage. The study, published Thursday (Nov. 19) in the journal Science , may help to solve a 150-year-old mystery in neuroscience. Nowadays, neuroscientists use cutting-edge tools to tease apart the junctions and wiring of our complex brains. But some basic theories in the field are far from new and rest on past discoveries. One of those theories concerns how the brain produces and comprehends speech. In the 1860s, German neuroanatomist Carl Wernicke identified an area of the brain that is critical to speech and usually found in the temporal lobe on the left side of the organ. Damage to Wernicke's area makes it challenging for people to understand what others are saying ‪—‬ a condition known as Wernicke's aphasia . Therefore, the brain region has been primarily thought of as a decoder that helps us break down the meaning of other people's speech. Wernicke's area (red) is found in the left temporal lobe. items.body: The immune system has several ways of remembering threats it's encountered and then mounting stronger defenses in the future. Now, a new study unpacks how cells keep one type of immune memory from fading, and the findings might matter for treating diseases like cancer and Alzheimer's disease. The research zoomed in on immune cells' epigenetics ‪—‬ the methods that cells use to control genes without changing their underlying DNA codes. This can involve changing how DNA is packaged inside cells, for example. DNA molecules are typically wound around tiny spools inside cells, and their gene activity depends on how tightly or loosely they're wound. Molecules called epigenetic markers can grab hold of the spool to tweak how the DNA is wound and thus activate or silence certain genes. Past research found epigenetic changes can prime immune cells against threats. The immune system's first line of defense — innate immune cells — can be switched into an activated state so they're ready to go if they encounter a germ. The findings, published Oct. 15 in The Astrophysical Journal Letters , could improve our understanding of the early solar system while reinforcing the Rubin Observatory's potential to unearth new cosmic objects during its brisk scans of the sky. Trojan asteroids are icy, rocky bodies that dwell in a planet's vicinity but don't orbit it. Instead, these asteroids orbit the sun, following the same path as the planet. Trojan asteroids exist in distinct swarms roughly 60 degrees ahead of and behind the planet. At these points, called Lagrange points 4 and 5 (L4 and L5), respectively, the gravitational tugs of the sun and the planet balance each other, essentially "locking" the asteroids in position, according to NASA . However, very few Trojans actually hang around for billions of years. Such asteroids are likely planetary building block remnants from the solar system's infancy, and detecting them in the outer solar system can be challenging. items.summary: On Wednesday (Nov. 18), NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft became the first human-made object to reach one light-day from Earth. Here, we look back at its most important discoveries, seen through groundbreaking space photos.
items.body: Early Wednesday (Nov. 18), NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft hit a new space exploration milestone: The probe, which launched in 1977, became the first spacecraft to reach one light-day from Earth. The milestone is largely symbolic, but it comes with practical consequences: While Voyager 1 cruises through interstellar space at roughly 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers) from our planet, it now takes a full 24 hours for radio signals moving at the speed of light to get from Voyager 1 to Earth, and vice versa. The growing space between Voyager and Earth makes it increasingly hard to troubleshoot problems on the nearly 50-year-old probe . But with Voyager 1 still collecting data with two of its science instruments, which are expected to stay powered up into the 2030s, NASA scientists say one thing is certain: The spacecraft isn't done surprising us. "What Voyager has taught me is to expect the unexpected," Linda Spilker , who joined the Voyager team in 1977 and is the mission's current project scientist, told Live Science in an interview. "Genetic differences between Neanderthals and modern humans still influence our brains today," study co-author Hugo Zeberg , an evolutionary geneticist at the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Germany, told Live Science. Zeberg and his colleague Svante Pääbo detailed their findings Nov. 16 in the journal PNAS . Before they went extinct around 40,000 years ago, Neanderthals were among the closest relatives of modern humans. Neanderthals' skulls were larger and more elongated than modern humans'. items.body: Homo erectus was adaptable enough to live in rainforests in what is now southern China and may have lived alongside Denisovans there, two new studies hint. The research is based on the incredibly rare findings of nine fossil teeth from ancient humans — eight from H. erectus and one from a mystery human in the genus Homo . The teeth reveal that H. erectus lived in China much more recently than previously thought and that this population likely devoured tropical food found there. "I think it's exciting because it means that there are two hominin populations occupying these rainforest conditions there at the same time," study first author Frido Welker , a molecular palaeoanthropologist at the University of Copenhagen in Denmark, told Live Science. H. erectus is generally seen as the first human species to venture out of Africa, after evolving about 2 million years ago. It spread through eastern Eurasia, reaching China and Indonesia between about 1.6 million and 1.8 million years ago. items.body: Archaeologists have unearthed a massive 2,000-year-old tomb of an elite nomad from the Xiongnu Empire in Central Asia. The nine-level tomb contained more than 400 grave goods and is the largest Xiongnu tomb ever found in Mongolia. Archaeologists identified the enormous tomb full of riches during a four-year excavation at the site of Duurlig Nars in northern Mongolia, according to a translated statement from the National Museum of Korea, whose researchers have been excavating the site in cooperation with the Institute of Archaeology of the Mongolian Academy of Sciences and the National Museum of Mongolia. Duurlig Nars is the largest noble burial complex of the Xiongnu Empire, with nearly 300 ancient burial mounds called kurgans. The Xiongnu, also known as the Hunnu, were a collection of nomadic tribes who coalesced into a mobile empire on the Mongolian steppe in 209 B.C. The Xiongnu were connected to a broad trading network that stretched from the Roman Empire in the West to China and the Korean Peninsula in the East. items.title: For centuries, we drew the pregnant body without a head. Now we need to fill in what we left blank.
items.summary: We need to understand how motherhood changes the brain, says neuroscientist Susana Carmona.
items.body: Look closely at the medical illustrations used in textbooks to depict the physiological changes of pregnancy, and you'll notice something strange: The bodies often have no heads. Generations of physicians learned to picture the pregnant patient as a torso — a uterus, a placenta, a growing belly — with everything above the neck left blank. That blank space is not an oversight by the illustrator. It is a faithful map of what medicine chose to study. We need to move on and create a complete picture of what happens during and after pregnancy so we can develop measures to prevent maternal deaths. For hundreds of years, we have devoted enormous effort to characterizing how pregnancy remodels nearly every organ and system in the body: the cardiovascular changes, the recalibration of the immune system, the metabolic adjustments — most of them orchestrated by hormones the placenta pours into the bloodstream. items.title: CERN physicists measure the universe at the smallest scale ever: enter the 'zeptoverse'
items.summary: Physicists at the Large Hadron Collider have detected a rare, 1-in-10-billion particle interaction that opens a view into the 'zeptoverse,' the smallest distance scale ever measured.
items.body: Using the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), the world's largest particle accelerator, scientists have gotten the first glimpse of the "zeptoverse" — the universe as it behaves within less than a hundred-trillionth of a wavelength of visible light, the smallest scale that researchers have explored to date. The new findings may one day help to answer long-standing cosmic mysteries, such as why there is far more matter than antimatter seen in the universe , and what makes up the dark matter that constitutes about 85% of all matter in the universe, the researchers announced Nov. 3 at a seminar at CERN (the European Organization for Nuclear Research), the organization that operates the LHC. The study, available as a preprint , has not yet been peer reviewed. At the LHC, located near Geneva at the border of France and Switzerland, researchers were investigating elusive particles called beauty quarks . These subatomic particles are cousins of the standard "up" and "down" quarks that make up the cores of all atoms in the universe. items.title: Grizzlies could thrive in California — so why aren’t we reintroducing them?
items.summary: In this excerpt from "Start With a Bear," author and environmental historian Peter S. Alagona looks at the models used to develop the U.S. grizzly bear recovery program, and how California could make an ideal home for a new population.
items.body: Computer models are widely used in ecological research and conservation, providing scientists with tools to predict how a given species might respond to a stressor or shift in conditions. These models can then be refined and built upon with real world data to get a better understanding of what's going on within a population and what the biggest risks are. But models aren't perfect. In this excerpt from " Start With a Bear: Humans, Grizzlies, and the Power of Stories on a Crowded Planet " (HarperOne, 2026), author Peter S. Alagona highlights how these models are built on the presumptions of their creators. Alagona examines the model of grizzly bear ( Ursus arctos horribilis ) habitats used by the Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) to inform its recovery plan for the species — and why California, despite its apparent suitability, was left out. Most of the grizzly habitat models that were introduced in the 1990s and 2000s, and then improved in the 2010s and 2020s, make two key assumptions. items.title: The Leonid meteor shower peaks tonight: How to see more than a dozen 'shooting stars' per hour
items.summary: Up to 15 shooting stars per hour may be visible as the Leonids peak under dark skies tonight (Nov. 16 - 17), with the moon setting before the best viewing hours.
items.body: One of November's best meteor showers peaks tonight (Nov. 16-17) and is expected to bring up to 15 "shooting stars" per hour to a near-moonless night sky. Although the annual Leonid meteor shower, which is famous for occasionally producing spectacular meteor storms, is active from Nov. 6 to Nov. 30, the peak on Monday into Tuesday is the best time to look, according to the American Meteor Society . Although the Leonids typically produce around 15 meteors per hour under ideal conditions, they're among the year's fastest shooting stars, reaching 43 miles per second (70 kilometers per second), and often produce bright meteors that leave glowing trails. The best time to see them is between midnight and dawn Tuesday (Nov. 17), when the constellation Leo, from which the meteors appear to radiate, climbs higher in the eastern sky. However, shooting stars can appear anywhere in the sky. A 45%-lit waxing crescent moon will set just before midnight, leaving dark skies for meteor watching. For the best views, find a spot away from artificial lights, lie back with a wide view of the sky, and allow about 20 minutes for your eyes to become adapted to the dark. items.title: Tiny robots can tumble through blood vessels to help dissolve blood clots, early test shows
items.summary: In recent animal tests, tiny robots released into the bloodstream showed promise for treating blood clots.
items.body: Microrobots controlled by magnets can sweep drugs towards hard-to-reach blood clots in the body, boosting the efficacy of these life-saving treatments, early tests in animals suggest. In tests with pigs, the microbots helped to dissolve clots around 10 times faster than medication alone. The research team is now working on further safety testing to ready the technology for eventual human trials. "The whole construct is inspired by nature," said lead researcher Simone Schürle , professor of medical microsystems at ETH Zürich. "There are these tiny bacteria that have little magnetic backbones which they use to navigate with the Earth's magnetic field, and we were really struck by the physics and the properties of them when exposed to rotating magnetic fields," Schürle told Live Science. ETH Zürich announced the research in a statement on Nov. 9. It has not been described in a peer-reviewed study yet. (Image credit: National Museum of Romanian History) QUICK FACTS Name: Thinkers of Cernavodă What they are: Clay figurines Where they are from: Cernavodă, Romania When they were made: Circa 5000 B.C. In 1956, archaeologists unearthed two unique figurines from one grave while excavating a Stone Age cemetery in southeast Romania. The unusual figurines — known as the Thinkers of Cernavodă or the Thinker and the Seated Woman — were made by people from the Hamangia culture and may be linked to ancient astronomical beliefs. The Thinkers of Cernavodă are in the collection of the National Museum of Romanian History and are a key part of the country's cultural heritage. They were crafted from fired clay and measure about 4.5 inches (11.5 centimeters) tall. The two figurines may represent a man (the Thinker) and a woman (the Seated Woman), according to the museum.
